taxonomic_note: Current Kew recognizes subsp. hallii and subsp. filipes; B009 remains species-level pending a need for subspecies-level field instruction.
look_here_first: HALL'S PANICGRASS: Look first for a small stiff, often blue-green perennial basal tuft with curled old leaves and an orderly open 6–20 cm panicle. Six physically archived exact-species photos now include Jim Conrad's actual Uvalde limestone-site tufts and WHITE TRUE LIGULE HAIR FRINGE at the leaf/sheath junction. The photographed hair fringe is a real field clue, NOT a ruler-verified 1–1.5 mm measurement or proof of a connected Hays root crown. Confirm the glossy awnless fertile lemma and glumes from measured mature spikelets; separate from hairy annual witchgrass, introduced kleingrass and switchgrass.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Panicum hallii, lists Texas as native, and recognizes subsp. hallii and subsp. filipes. Hagenbuch & Lemke explicitly record multiple Hays County specimens. The same appendix records Blanco County (Lackey 777, SWT). The same appendix records Val Verde County (Labus 301, 326, 352, SWT). Kerr — Singhurst et al. (2010), Kerr Wildlife Management Area natural flora, p. 511, published specimens JS 10677; FG 8249; LS 4050, 4416, 4532. Together Hays, Blanco, Kerr satisfy the 3-county project threshold; historical out-of-zone counties not counted.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Occurrence is not treated as nativity; introduced records do not count toward the three-county native threshold.

morphology_keys.joey_family_training: Use the completed Poaceae morphology framework: inflorescence architecture first, then spikelets, glumes, lemma/palea, awns, ligule, collar, sheath and nodes.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Ripe ~2–4 mm spikelet with lower glume and upper shiny fertile floret at scale
crew_field_check: HALL'S PANICGRASS: Native small mostly BASAL, stiff blue-green perennial BUNCH (often around 30–60 cm); old basal leaves curl like wood shavings. Flower stalk bears an open but modest ~6–20 cm panicle with stiffer ascending branches and small clustered ovoid spikelets. Confirm a mature spikelet, the shiny fertile lemma and ciliate/hair-fringe ligule with a lens. The existing 3 original photographs teach tuft, leaf curling and actual spikelet; not microscopic anatomy.

Witchgrass P. capillare is a hairy ANNUAL and much more cloudlike; Kleingrass P. coloratum is a robust African-introduced forage perennial; switchgrass P. virgatum is usually much taller, rhizomatous and has a conspicuous white triangular blade-base hair patch.
Examine the same plant's crown, collar and mature spikelet with a millimeter scale before assigning difficult specimens.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Panicum virgatum: Switchgrass is much taller and rhizomatous with a much larger diffuse panicle. Panicum capillare: Witchgrass is annual and strongly hairy with a huge lax panicle; Hall's is perennial, glaucous and stiffer.
comparisons.field_lesson: Witchgrass P. capillare is a hairy ANNUAL and much more cloudlike; Kleingrass P. coloratum is a robust African-introduced forage perennial; switchgrass P. virgatum is usually much taller, rhizomatous and has a conspicuous white triangular blade-base hair patch.

The photographed hair fringe is a real field clue, NOT a ruler-verified 1–1.5 mm measurement or proof of a connected Hays root crown. field_id_finish_pass.comparison_key: Witchgrass P. capillare is a hairy ANNUAL and much more cloudlike; Kleingrass P. coloratum is a robust African-introduced forage perennial; switchgrass P. virgatum is usually much taller, rhizomatous and has a conspicuous white triangular blade-base hair patch.
measured_macro_photo_targets: Connected rooted Hays-area perennial crown with complete attached flowering culm and centimeter scale
True photographed hair-fringe ligule on the same specimen with 1-mm calibration; existing Uvalde source ligule is unscaled
At least two ripe 2.2–3.9 mm spikelets with separately measured glumes, sterile lemma and shiny awnless fertile lemma

measured_species_key_20261023.look_here_first: Look for a small mostly basal stiff, often blue-green perennial tuft; older basal blades curl like wood shavings. Trace a 6–20 cm open but stiff-branched panicle and inspect clustered, appressed oval spikelets. Confirm the short fringed ligule and shiny hard mature fertile lemma rather than guessing from a seedhead silhouette.
measured_species_key_20261023.growth_form: Perennial bunchgrass with persistent basal sheaths and mostly basal leaves; culms 20–80 cm in Kew, often 30–60 cm in Texas field descriptions. No long creeping stolon or extensive rhizome is established by the existing photographs.
measured_species_key_20261023.ligule_collar: Kew GrassBase: ligule a 1–1.5 mm fringe of hairs. Williamson County's subsp. filipes treatment: a 1.2–1.5 mm membranous ligule ciliate from midpoint or below, whitish collar to 1.5 mm. At the attached blade/sheath junction photograph the membrane and hairs separately; do not use subsp. filipes details to assign a subspecies to the species-level card.
measured_species_key_20261023.flowering_architecture: Open pyramidal 6–20 cm panicle with ascending, relatively stiff branches; short-pedicelled solitary/appressed spikelets may overlap in small clusters. Unlike loose tumble-like witchgrass, the flowering head is relatively compact and orderly.
measured_species_key_20261023.spikelet_glume_lemma_awn: Kew species-level: dorsally compressed ovate spikelets 2.2–3.7(–3.9) mm, one lower sterile and one upper fertile floret; lower glume one-third to two-thirds spikelet length, upper glume approximately full spikelet length, each described as 5-veined; lower sterile lemma approximately spikelet length; hardened shiny dark-brown fertile lemma 2–3.5 mm, awnless. The Williamson County subsp. filipes specimen differs (2.1–3 mm spikelets, upper glume 7–11 veins, fertile lemma 1.5–1.8 mm); keep these taxon-concept-specific observations separate.
measured_species_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: P. capillare (witchgrass): hairy annual with broad cloudlike, often detached/tumbling panicle, rather than stiff basal perennial tuft. P. coloratum (kleingrass): robust introduced forage perennial with larger coarse growth and its own glume proportions. P. virgatum (switchgrass): taller often rhizomatous and with blade-base hairs; compare intact basal crown, ligule and mature spikelets.
diagnostic_photo_arrow_gaps: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one connected rooted perennial crown with basal curled dry leaves and cm scale.
NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: exposed true 1–1.5 mm ligule at attached blade/sheath junction with 1-mm scale, separating membrane from cilia.
NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: two or more mature 2.2–3.9 mm spikelets, glumes separated and veins visible, 1-mm scale at 10–20×.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Hall's panicgrass — photograph-guided field recognition
steps: START with the physically archived whole-habit photograph: trace the relatively small mostly basal perennial tuft and stiff ascending panicle branches; do not infer a rhizome from the photo.
LOOK at the physically archived curled-leaf photograph. Old basal blades can curl tightly, a supporting vegetative cue rather than proof of species identity.

FOLLOW a panicle branch to the actual small oval spikelets in the archived reproductive close-up. Arrows already point to visibly resolved spikelets, but individual glumes cannot be counted at this resolution.

ACTUAL LIGULE PHOTO NOW AVAILABLE: species panel 6 (index 5) shows the white true hair fringe at the leaf/sheath junction with two visible arrows; the source image lacks a 1-mm ruler, so measure a new attached collar under 10–20× before teaching 1–1.5 mm as photographically demonstrated.

FIELD MACRO HOLD: photograph intact mature 2.2–3.9 mm spikelets against a millimeter scale, then separated glumes, sterile floret and glossy hardened awnless fertile lemma. Keep species-level characters separate from subsp. filipes measurements.

CHECK the look-alikes: witchgrass (P. capillare) tends to be a hairy annual with a diffuse cloudlike panicle; introduced kleingrass (P. coloratum) is usually much coarser; switchgrass (P. virgatum) is typically taller and often rhizomatous.

NEW VERIFIED GITHUB-HOSTED CC0 IMAGE: Patrick Alexander's separated glossy mature fruiting units are shown at high resolution; teach the smooth hardened appearance, but these are not a calibrated dissection exposing both glumes or the true ligule.

NEW ACTUAL UVALDE MACRO: Jim Conrad photographed attached green narrow spikelets with repeated veins and separate detached pale mature units on a fingertip. Neither proves exact glume, fertile lemma or 1-mm spikelet size; do not add invisible arrows.

NEW BLANCO COUNTY PRESSED VOUCHER: the USDA ARS source-confirmed CC0 photo NA0084210 shows a physical fibrous root system still attached to a flattened grass tuft and flowering culms. This is a PRESERVED HERBARIUM SPECIMEN, not a living grass photographed rooted in the soil, and does not substitute for a fresh 1-mm leaf collar or a spikelet dissection.

FINE ANATOMY ORIGINALS: Bob Harms's actual same-species inner ligule/sheath photo shows pale tissue at the junction and a ruler; his second photo shows separated mature reproductive bracts and smooth inner units. BOTH are true P. hallii, but don't claim every bract is a specific lemma/glume until keyed and measured.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Small blue-green perennial basal tuft + relatively orderly ascending-branched panicle + measured true hairy/ciliate ligule and hard shiny mature fertile lemma. No single habit photograph proves the species.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Eleven Hall's panicgrass exact-species archives: true Uvalde hairy ligule and flowering macros, USDA Blanco pressed connected roots, plus two Bob Harms real collar and separated reproductive plates under author-granted EDUCATIONAL use (not CC). Still need a living rooted crown, independently keyed scale-calibrated individual glumes and live mobile arrow QA.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SHORT BLUE-GREEN TUFT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Mostly basal stiff glaucous perennial bunch; old dry basal blades often curl.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Species panels 1–2 (indices 0–1) show a compact basal habit and curling dry blades; the new Jim Conrad Uvalde limestone-site panel 5 (index 4) independently shows small real tufts among rocks. Neither photograph exposes a connected rooted perennial crown. Kew reports 20–80 cm culms; trace a complete flowering stem before determining species.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL TARGET HABIT PHOTOS — ROOTED CROWN WITH SCALE NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE LIGULE AND LEAF COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Kew: 1–1.5 mm fringe of hairs; verify at the blade–sheath junction.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Jim Conrad's source-authenticated Uvalde photograph (species panel 6, index 5) ACTUALLY SHOWS a white fringe of true ligule hairs at the blade/sheath junction, with the comparatively smooth green sheath below; two arrows target these visible tissues. This is genuine anatomical photo evidence but the original is unscaled, so the Kew species-level 1–1.5 mm hair-fringe length remains a PUBLISHED measurement, not photo-measured. A Williamson County subsp. filipes treatment describes a 1.2–1.5 mm membranous ciliate ligule and pale collar; do not impose subspecies-specific morphology or identity on this species-level photo. Still obtain a calibrated 1-mm collar image of a connected local specimen.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ACTUAL TRUE LIGULE HAIR FRINGE PHOTO + TWO VISIBLE ARROWS; 1-MM SCALE AND CONNECTED HAYS VOUCHER MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN BUT ORDERLY FLOWERING PANICLE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Pyramidal 6–20 cm panicle with relatively stiff ascending branches.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Species panel 3 (index 2) shows actual branch architecture and small attached spikelets, with existing arrows only on visible units. Kew reports appressed solitary spikelets; Williamson subsp. filipes specimens can show short paired stalks, so do not force an unexamined subspecies arrangement onto this species card. A very diffuse detached/tumbling annual head suggests P. capillare instead.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL ARCHIVED BRANCH PHOTO — NO MEASURED DISSECTION

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · SPIKELET, GLUMES, LEMMA AND AWNS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Spikelet 2.2–3.7(–3.9) mm; lower glume 1/3–2/3, upper near full length.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Species-level Kew GrassBase describes dorsally compressed ovate two-floret spikelets, five-veined lower and upper glumes, a basal sterile floret and an upper fertile floret with shiny dark-brown hardened lemma ~2–3.5 mm. The fertile lemma is awnless. The Williamson County subsp. filipes treatment gives DIFFERENT narrower measurements and glume-vein counts; keep those subspecies-specific. Species panel 4 (index 3) shows real glossy mature units but cannot prove all glume veins or millimeter lengths.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL GLOSSY FRUIT PHOTO — MEASURED GLUME/LEMMA DISSECTION NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · PRACTICAL LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Contrast annual witchgrass, introduced kleingrass, and robust switchgrass.
field_id_short_tiles.details: P. capillare is a hairy annual with a much more diffuse cloudlike head (different-species comparison panel 7, index 6, NOT Hall's panicgrass). Introduced P. coloratum is generally a coarser perennial forage grass; P. virgatum commonly has a taller rhizomatous base and conspicuous white blade-base hairs. Compare the true photographed Hall's ligule (index 5), rooted habit and mature spikelet. Neither a panicle silhouette nor blue-green color alone is decisive.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL WITCHGRASS COMPARISON — MATCHED ANATOMY MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND PHOTO/QA HANDOFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: six archived exact-species JPEGs; measured reproductive dissection and connected root still missing.
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish owning lane): same-specimen Hays-area connected rooted perennial crown, flowering stem and centimeter ruler; calibrated true 1–1.5-mm hair-fringe ligule/collar beside 1-mm scale (unscaled Uvalde ligule already photographed at index 5); two ripe 2.2–3.9-mm spikelets with individually separated glumes, sterile lemma and hard glossy awnless fertile lemma at 10–20×; matched local P. capillare, P. coloratum and P. virgatum comparisons where available. Preserve taxonomy/subspecies/county holds; do not claim measured anatomy or FINISHED from unscaled photos.
